```{r}
#| echo: false

library(knitr)
library(formatR)
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggtext)
library(gridExtra, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

options(width = 60)
opts_chunk$set(out.width = '100%')

opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)
opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, comment = '', class.output = 'sh',
               fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center")

options(useFancyQuotes = FALSE)

my_red <- "#E41A1C"
my_blue <- "#377EB8"
my_green <- "#4DAF4A"
my_purple <- "#984EA3"
my_orange <- "#FF7F00"
my_yellow <- "#FFFF33"
my_red2 <- "#FBB4AE" 
my_blue2 <- "#B3CDE3" 
my_green2 <- "#CCEBC5" 
my_purple2 <- "#DECBE4"
my_orange2 <- "#FED9A6"
my_yellow2 <- "#FFFFCC"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper functions (these replace the TikZ drawing / overlay code in the .Rmd)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# --- Venn diagrams (replaces the TikZ circles) ------------------------------
# y circle is fixed at (0, 0); x1 and x2 circles sit at (-d, -1.5) and (d, -1.5)
make_venn <- function(d, x1_lab, x2_lab, arrow_x,
                      bottom = c("Variance of <i>y</i> predicted",
                                 "by both <i>x</i><sub>1</sub> and <i>x</i><sub>2</sub>"),
                      note = NULL, note_x = 4, note_y = c(-3, -3.5),
                      r = 1.5, n = 600) {

  cy  <- c(0, 0)
  cx1 <- c(-d, -1.5)
  cx2 <- c(d, -1.5)

  # circle outlines
  tt <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 300)
  circ <- function(cc, g) data.frame(x = cc[1] + r * cos(tt), y = cc[2] + r * sin(tt), group = g)
  circles <- rbind(circ(cy, "y"), circ(cx1, "x1"), circ(cx2, "x2"))

  # fill each distinct region on a fine grid
  grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = n), y = seq(-3.2, 1.7, length.out = n))
  in_y  <- (grid$x - cy[1])^2  + (grid$y - cy[2])^2  <= r^2
  in_x1 <- (grid$x - cx1[1])^2 + (grid$y - cx1[2])^2 <= r^2
  in_x2 <- (grid$x - cx2[1])^2 + (grid$y - cx2[2])^2 <= r^2
  fill <- rep(NA_character_, nrow(grid))
  fill[in_x1 & !in_y & !in_x2] <- my_red
  fill[in_x2 & !in_y & !in_x1] <- my_yellow
  fill[in_y & !in_x1 & !in_x2] <- my_blue
  fill[in_y & in_x1 & !in_x2]  <- my_purple   # y and x1 only
  fill[in_y & in_x2 & !in_x1]  <- my_green    # y and x2 only
  fill[in_x1 & in_x2 & !in_y]  <- my_orange   # x1 and x2 only
  fill[in_y & in_x1 & in_x2]   <- "#808080"   # all three
  grid$fill <- fill

  # labels inside the circles
  labs_df <- data.frame(
    x = c(0, x1_lab[1], x2_lab[1]),
    y = c(0.3, x1_lab[2], x2_lab[2]),
    label = c("<b><i>y</i></b>", "<b><i>x</i><sub>1</sub></b>", "<b><i>x</i><sub>2</sub></b>")
  )

  # annotation text (one row per line of text, as in the TikZ nodes)
  txt <- data.frame(
    x = c(0, 0, -4, -4, 4, 4),
    y = c(3, 2.5, 1, 0.5, 1, 0.5),
    label = c("Variance of <i>y</i> not",
              "predicted by <i>x</i><sub>1</sub> or <i>x</i><sub>2</sub>",
              "Variance of <i>y</i> uniquely",
              "predicted by <i>x</i><sub>1</sub>",
              "Variance of <i>y</i> uniquely",
              "predicted by <i>x</i><sub>2</sub>"),
    color = "black"
  )
  txt <- rbind(txt, data.frame(x = 0, y = c(-4, -4.5)[seq_along(bottom)],
                               label = bottom, color = "black"))
  if (!is.null(note)) {
    txt <- rbind(txt, data.frame(x = note_x, y = note_y[seq_along(note)],
                                 label = note, color = my_blue))
  }

  arrows <- data.frame(
    x    = c(0, -3.5, 3.5, 0),
    y    = c(2.25, 0.25, 0.25, -3.7),
    xend = c(0, -arrow_x, arrow_x, 0),
    yend = c(1, -0.5, -0.5, -1)
  )

  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = fill)) +
    scale_fill_identity(na.value = "transparent") +
    geom_path(data = circles, aes(x = x, y = y, group = group),
              color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_richtext(data = labs_df, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
                  size = 7, fill = NA, label.color = NA) +
    geom_richtext(data = txt, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, color = color),
                  size = 4.3, fill = NA, label.color = NA) +
    scale_color_identity() +
    geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                 linewidth = 0.8, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), angle = 20)) +
    coord_fixed(xlim = c(-6.3, 6.3), ylim = c(-5, 3.6), clip = "off") +
    theme_void() +
    theme(legend.position = "none", plot.margin = margin(5, 5, 5, 5))
}

# --- Custom HTML for annotated R output (replaces TikZ overlays on output) ----

emit_html <- function(x) cat("```{=html}\n", x, "\n```\n", sep = "")

# an outlined, rounded highlight around a piece of text
hl_span <- function(txt, color) {
  sprintf('<span style="box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px %s; border-radius: 0.6em; padding: 0 2px;">%s</span>',
          color, htmltools::htmlEscape(txt))
}

# R console-style output block built from HTML lines (one <span> per line)
out_block <- function(lines_html, font_px = NULL, line_px = NULL) {
  st <- ""
  if (!is.null(font_px)) st <- sprintf("font-size:%spx; line-height:%spx;", font_px, line_px)
  lines_html[lines_html == ""] <- "&nbsp;"
  paste0('<div class="cell-output cell-output-stdout"><pre style="', st, '">',
         '<code style="max-height:none; overflow:visible;">',
         paste0('<span style="display:block;">', lines_html, '</span>', collapse = ""),
         '</code></pre></div>')
}

# circle the printed value that belongs to `name` in a printed named vector
hl_named_vector <- function(out, name, color) {
  html <- htmltools::htmlEscape(out)
  for (i in seq_len(length(out) - 1)) {
    m <- regexpr(paste0("(?<![A-Za-z0-9])", name, "(?![A-Za-z0-9])"), out[i], perl = TRUE)
    if (m > 0) {
      e <- as.integer(m) + nchar(name) - 1
      v <- out[i + 1]
      left <- substr(v, 1, e)
      ts <- as.integer(regexpr("[^ ]+$", left))
      html[i + 1] <- paste0(htmltools::htmlEscape(substr(v, 1, ts - 1)),
                            hl_span(substr(left, ts, e), color),
                            htmltools::htmlEscape(substr(v, e + 1, nchar(v))))
    }
  }
  html
}

# line + arrowhead (arrowhead sits at the start point x0, y0)
arrow_svg <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, color, len = 18, half_w = 8) {
  ang <- atan2(y1 - y0, x1 - x0)
  bx <- x0 + len * cos(ang); by <- y0 + len * sin(ang)
  px <- -sin(ang); py <- cos(ang)
  sprintf('<line x1="%.1f" y1="%.1f" x2="%.1f" y2="%.1f" stroke="%s" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="%.1f,%.1f %.1f,%.1f %.1f,%.1f" fill="%s"/>',
          x0, y0, x1, y1, color,
          x0, y0, bx + half_w * px, by + half_w * py, bx - half_w * px, by - half_w * py, color)
}
```

## Categorical Predictors

::: {style="font-size: 0.775em;"}

So far, we have discussed regression with continuous predictors

It is also possible to use categorical predictors in regression models, or both categorical and continuous predictors

A regression model with **only** categorical predictors is identical to a technique we have already learned. What is it?

- [One-way or factorial ANOVA!]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [**Technically:**]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [ANOVA refers to the method of comparing variance attributable to different predictors/IVs (hence Analysis of Variance)]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
      - [One-way and factorial ANOVA are specific types of ANOVA for one or more categorical IVs]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [Regression refers to the method of estimating a general linear model (usually ordinary least squares)]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
      - [General linear models can have any mix of continuous or categorical predictors]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
      - [Comparing regression models by adding or removing predictors is also a type of ANOVA]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
      
:::

## Example

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}


Performance (math) IQ predicted by verbal IQ and sex (among patients recovering from a coma)

* criterion: performance (math) IQ---continuous

* predictor 1: verbal IQ---continuous

* predictor 2: sex (female, male)---categorical

Solution: code females as '0', males as '1' (could also be the other way around)

* Could also use different numbers, but '0' and '1' lend to the easiest interpretations

:::

```{r}
# Annotated regression output: highlighted coefficient rows, arrows, and callouts
options(width = 60)
fit_wong <- lm(piq ~ viq + sex, Wong)
out <- gsub("\t", "  ", capture.output(summary(fit_wong)))
out <- out[cumsum(nzchar(out)) > 0]            # drop leading blank line(s)
out <- out[seq_len(max(which(nzchar(out))))]   # drop trailing blank line(s)

lh <- 24            # line height (px)
fs <- 17            # font size (px)
w  <- 660           # width of the output box (px)
callout_x <- 730    # left edge of the callouts (px)

pats     <- c("^\\(Intercept\\)", "^viq", "^sexMale")
cols     <- c(my_blue, my_orange, my_purple)
idx      <- sapply(pats, function(p) grep(p, out)[1])
target_y <- c(192, 300, 408)     # vertical centre of each callout (px)

line_html <- vapply(seq_along(out), function(i) {
  txt <- if (nchar(out[i]) == 0) "&nbsp;" else htmltools::htmlEscape(out[i])
  k <- match(i, idx)
  extra <- if (is.na(k)) "" else
    sprintf("box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 3px %s; background: %s26;", cols[k], cols[k])
  sprintf('<div style="height:%dpx; line-height:%dpx; %s">%s</div>', lh, lh, extra, txt)
}, character(1))

arrows_html <- paste(
  mapply(function(i, ty, col) arrow_svg(w, (i - 0.5) * lh, callout_x - 10, ty, col),
         idx, target_y, cols),
  collapse = "")

callouts <- c("Intercept:<br>Predicted PIQ for<br>female with VIQ = 0",
              "Predicted increase in PIQ for a<br>one-point increase in VIQ,<br>holding sex constant",
              "Predicted decrease in<br>PIQ for males, holding<br>VIQ constant")
callout_html <- sprintf(
  '<div style="position:absolute; left:%dpx; top:%dpx; color:%s; font-size:20px; line-height:28px; white-space:nowrap;">%s</div>',
  callout_x, target_y - 42, cols, callouts)

emit_html(paste0(
  '<div style="position:absolute; left:0; top:0; width:', w,
  'px; box-sizing:border-box; padding:0 10px; background:#f5f5f5; border-radius:6px; ',
  'font-family:SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Monaco,Consolas,monospace; font-size:', fs,
  'px; white-space:pre; overflow:hidden;">', paste(line_html, collapse = ""), '</div>',
  '<svg width="1500" height="520" style="position:absolute; left:0; top:0; pointer-events:none; overflow:visible;">',
  arrows_html, '</svg>',
  paste(callout_html, collapse = "")
))
```

## Dummy Coding Review

For $k$ groups, we can represent group membership with ($k-1$) dichotomous dummy variables

For each dummy variable, assign '1' to members of one group and '0' to all others

One group (called the reference group) is coded '0' on all dummy variables

Example:

| Group | $x_{1}$ | $x_{2}$ | $x_{3}$ |
|:----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Control | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Drug | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Therapy | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Drug + Therapy | 0 | 0 | 1 |

## Dummy Coded Model

::: {style="font-size: 0.77em;"}

Regression model:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3x_3 + b_4\text{age}$$

::::: columns

:::: column

* Control: $\hat{y} = b_0+ b_4\text{age}$ 

* Drug: $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1+ b_4\text{age}$

* Therapy: $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_2x_2+ b_4\text{age}$

* D + T: $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_3x_3+ b_4\text{age}$

::::

:::: column

| Group | $x_{1}$ | $x_{2}$ | $x_{3}$ |
|:----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Control | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| Drug | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Therapy | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Drug + Therapy | 0 | 0 | 1 |

::::

:::::

Interpretation:

* $b_0 + b_4\text{age}$: predicted $\hat{y}$ for control group
* $b_1 + b_4\text{age}$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between (drug) and (control) holding age constant
* $b_2 + b_4\text{age}$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between (therapy) and (control) holding age constant
* $b_3 + b_4\text{age}$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between (drug + therapy) and (control) holding age constant

<!-- Cool side effect: $x_1$, $x_2$, and $x_3$ are uncorrelated! -->

<!-- * If $n$ is equal for each group -->

:::

## Dummy Coded Tests

Test of individual predictors:

* If $b_1$ is significant, then the $x_1$ group (drug group) differs significantly from the control group (contrast coding, excluding other groups)

* Degrees of freedom for the one-way ANOVA ( = #groups - 1) are divided into (#groups - 1) contrasts comparing each group to the reference group

Test of $R^2$

* Equivalent to the omnibus test for the one-way ANOVA!

* Test the hypothesis that all coefficients are simultaneously zero

## Effects Coding Review

As with dummy variables, for $k$ groups, we need $k-1$ effect variables

Each effect code consists of '1' for members of one group, '-1' for members of another group, and '0' for the remaining groups

The same group receives the '-1' effect for each effect variables

For example:

| Group | $x_{1}$ | $x_{2}$ | $x_{3}$ |
|:----------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Control | -1 | -1 | -1 |
| Drug | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Therapy | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| Drug + Therapy | 0 | 0 | 1 |

## Effects Coded Model

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Regression model:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3x_3 + b_4\text{age}$$

Interpretation:

* $b_0 + b_4\text{age}$: predicted mean of $y$ at for a given age

* $b_1$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between drug and mean $y$ holding age constant

* $b_2$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between therapy and mean $y$ holding age constant

* $b_3$: difference in $\hat{y}$ between (drug + therapy) and mean $y$ holding age constant

Omnibus test of $R^2$ is equivalent to simultaneously testing main effects in ANOVA

ANOVA interaction corresponds to **moderation** effects---stay tuned!

:::

## Model Selection Revisited

Last time, we got a taste of the multiple ways to specify a model

Model building using regression is an art:

* We should include ("control for") relevant predictors
  
* We should also strive for the simplest model possible
  
* Don't want to include redundant (or nearly redundant) predictors

## SAT Example Revisited

Last time we looked at a model predicting average SAT scores from educational expenditures and the (log of) the percentage of students in each state who took the SAT.

* 50 observations (one for each U.S. state)

* Data from the 1994-1995 school year

```{r}
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
dat <- readxl::read_xlsx("../../data/States.xlsx", sheet = 1)
dat <- dat |> mutate(logPctSAT = log(PctSAT)) 
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

lm2 <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, dat)
coef(lm2)
```

## Consequences

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Multicollinearity is the extent to which predictors are correlated with other predictors in a regression model

Consequences of severe (high) multicollinearity:

1. Partial regression coefficients have large standard errors
  
    + Consider:

    $$s_{b_1} = \frac{s_y}{s_{x_1}}\sqrt{\frac{1-R^2}{(N-p-1){\color{#377EB8}\boxed{(1-r_{x_1,x_2}^2)}}}} \qquad {\color{#377EB8}\begin{array}{l}\text{When } r_{x_1,x_2} \text{ is large,} \\ s_{b_1} \text{ is large}\end{array}}$$

    + Low statistical power of partial regression coefficients
    
2.  In extreme cases, results cannot be calculated (no unique solution to the OLS equations)
  
    + This will always occur if $p > N - 1$, and sometimes with fewer predictors

:::

## Variance Inflation Factor

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

Two collinearity statistics:

* Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)

* Tolerance = 1 / VIF

* Just different ways of framing the same statistic

VIF for $x_j = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}$

* $R^2_j$, $j = 1, \ldots, p$ is the $R^2$ value from the regression of $x_j$ (treating $x_j$ as the DV) on all other predictors in the regression model

If the model we care about is

$$y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \epsilon$$

Then $R^2_1$ is the $R^2$ for this model:

$$x_1 = \beta_{(1),0} +  \beta_{(1),1} x_2 + \beta_{(1),2}x_3 + \epsilon_{(1)}$$

:::

## VIF And Tolerance

* VIF is how much the standard error increases due to multicolinearity for that predictor

    - Example: VIF = 1.057 means that our estimate for $s_{b_1}$ is 1.057 times as large as it would be if $x_1$ were uncorrelated with the other predictors ($R^2_1 = 0$)

* Tolerance is the inverse of VIF: proportion of variance of $x_j$ that is independent of other predictors


Rules of thumb:

* VIF > 5 (tolerance < .2) indicates high multicollinearity
* VIF > 10 (tolerance < .1) indicates serious multicollinearity



## Variance in `R`

For only two predictors, the VIF associated with each predictor will be the same

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false

library(car)
lm1 <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + PctSAT, dat)
vif(lm1)
```

For three or more predictors, the VIF is usually unique for each predictor

```{r}
#| echo: true

lm2 <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + PctSAT + Salary, dat)
vif(lm2)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

mod <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + PctSAT + Salary, dat)
vif(mod)
spcor(dat[, c("Expend", "PctSAT", "Salary")])$estimate
1 / (1 - .3905570^2)
```

## Tolerance

Two equivalent ways of calculating the tolerance:

1. Take the inverse of the VIF

```{r}
#| echo: true

1 / vif(lm2)
```

2. Take 1 - $R^2$ from separate linear regression models

```{r}
#| echo: true

1 - summary(lm(Expend ~ PctSAT + Salary, dat))$r.squared
1 - summary(lm(PctSAT ~ Expend + Salary, dat))$r.squared
1 - summary(lm(Salary ~ Expend + PctSAT, dat))$r.squared
```

## Assumptions

1. Fixed effects model

2. Conditional distributions are normally distributed with constant variance (homoscedasticity)

3. Independent and normally distributed residuals

4. Correct model specification

5. Perfectly reliable predictors

6. No multivariate outliers


## Model Usage Review

What are the three things we typically use models for? (Way back in lecture 12!)

1.  [**Describe:** A statistical model can help us understand data by summarizing variables or mapping relationships between different variables]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

2.  [**Predict:** A statistical model can help us anticipate how we expect **new** observations, which were not in our initial sample that we used to estimate the model, to look]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

3.  [**Decide:** A statistical model can guide how we choose to behave by helping us understand the likelihood of different consequences of our choices]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}




## Assumption Impacts



Assumptions (esp. 1 and 2) are the necessary conditions for **hypothesis tests** to have known properties (e.g., Type I error rate)

- Biggest impact on our **decision rules** for frequentist inference
  
- A bit less relevant when regression is used for description

- Can be relevant for prediction and non-frequentist decision-making

- All of these can affect results, so they are important to be aware and understand consequences of



## Fixed Effects Model

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

The multiple regression model treats predictors as **fixed**

* Interest is in specific predictors
* Predictors are systematically included in the sample and would be included in all sample replications
* e.g., attractiveness ratings on a *specific* photograph (rather than a randomly sampled photograph)

In contrast, **random effects models**

* Predictors are sampled from a distribution
* Examples: 
  
    + Attractiveness ratings on one of many photographs that could have been used
    + Time points in repeated-measures design

* Can be accommodated with multilevel regression models

:::

## Conditional Distributions

In fixed effects regression, we assume that predictors are fixed constants

For every combination of predictors, we have a distribution of $y$

* "Conditional distribution of $y$"

Assume that each conditional distribution

* Is normally distributed

* Has constant variance 

* Known as **homoscedasticity**
    - Extension of homogeneity of variance for **all values** of a continuous predictor rather than **discrete groups**

## With One Predictor

```{r}
set.seed(30)
n <- 100
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
y <- 2 + .5 * x + rnorm(n, sd = 1)
y1 <- seq(-2, 2, by = .1)
ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x, y)) + geom_abline(intercept = 2, slope = .5, color = my_green) +
  geom_path(aes(x = 2 + 2 * dnorm(y1), y = 2 + .5 * 2 + y1), color = my_blue) + 
  geom_path(aes(x = 4 + 2 * dnorm(y1), y = 2 + .5 * 4 + y1), color = my_blue) + 
  geom_path(aes(x = 6 + 2 * dnorm(y1), y = 2 + .5 * 6 + y1), color = my_blue) + 
  geom_path(aes(x = 8 + 2 * dnorm(y1), y = 2 + .5 * 8 + y1), color = my_blue) + 
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2, xend = 2 + 2 * dnorm(0), y = 3, yend = 3), color = my_blue, lty = 3) + 
  geom_segment(aes(x = 4, xend = 4 + 2 * dnorm(0), y = 4, yend = 4), color = my_blue, lty = 3) + 
  geom_segment(aes(x = 6, xend = 6 + 2 * dnorm(0), y = 5, yend = 5), color = my_blue, lty = 3) + 
  geom_segment(aes(x = 8, xend = 8 + 2 * dnorm(0), y = 6, yend = 6), color = my_blue, lty = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2, xend = 2, y = 1, yend = 5), color = my_blue, lty = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 4, xend = 4, y = 2, yend = 6), color = my_blue, lty = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 6, xend = 6, y = 3, yend = 7), color = my_blue, lty = 3) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 8, xend = 8, y = 4, yend = 8), color = my_blue, lty = 3) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = c(2, 4, 6, 8), y = c(3, 4, 5, 6)), color = my_red, size = 4, pch = 7) + 
  theme_light()
```

## Evaluation

**Homoscedasticity:** Scatterplot of residuals against each predictor separately

* If no heteroscedasticity, then residuals scatter uniformly across $x$ axis

* Loess lines with standard error band can be informative

**Normality:** Usual methods

* Skewness and kurtosis
  
* Histogram or kernel density plot with normal curve imposed
  
* QQ-plot

As $N$ increases, worry less about violations of normality

## Evaluating Homoscedasticity

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

mod <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, dat |> mutate(logPctSAT = log(PctSAT)))
p1 <- ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x = mod$model$Expend, y = mod$residuals), color = my_purple) + theme_light() + 
  labs(x = "Expenditure", y = "Residuals") + 
  geom_smooth(aes(x = mod$model$Expend, y = mod$residuals), method = "loess", col = my_blue) 
p2 <- ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x = mod$model$logPctSAT, y = mod$residuals), color = my_purple) + 
  theme_light() + labs(x = "log Percent SAT", y = "Residuals") + 
  geom_smooth(aes(x = mod$model$logPctSAT, y = mod$residuals), method = "loess", col = my_blue)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1)



```

## Interpretation

- The residuals (purple dots) have a larger spread in the middle range of `Expenditure`
- Tend to be smaller for large and small values
- Residuals much more homogenous across `log Percent SAT`

## QQ Plot

```{r}
ggplot() + geom_qq_line(aes(sample = mod$residuals), col = my_red) + 
  geom_qq(aes(sample = mod$residuals)) + theme_minimal() + 
  labs(x = "", y = "")
```

Thoughts? [Normality of residuals seems OK]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

## Conditional Distributions

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

What if **normality** is violated?

* Nonnormality does not bias estimated regression coefficients
* Nonnormality can increase standard errors of regression coefficients
* For small samples, $t$ tests (for regression coefficients) and $F$ test (for $R^2$) may be biased
* For moderate to large samples, effects of nonnormality on significance testing is small

What if **homoscedasticity** is violated?

* Heteroscedasticity *does not* bias estimated regression coefficients
* Heteroscedasticity *does* bias standard errors of regression coefficients
* Direction of bias depends on the relationship of the conditional variances to the predictor
    + If variance increases as predictor increases, standard error is underestimated and Type I error rates are inflated
    + If variance decreases as predictor increases, standard error is overestimated and Type I error rates are too low

:::

## Residuals

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

We also assume that **all residuals are independent of each other**

If observations are random, then residuals shouldn't be correlated

In some situations, residuals might be correlated. Examples:

* Observations from the same person at different times

    + Observations closer in time may be more related than those farther in time
    + Known as **temporal autocorrelation**
    + Repeated measures nested within individuals

* Observations from individuals in the same community

    + Observations from people who are geographically closer together may be more related than those from those from diverse geographic locations
    + Known as **spatial autocorrelation**
    + Individuals nested within communities

**Multilevel modeling** is a better method to handle these types of data

:::

## Residuals

What are the consequences of autocorrelation among residuals across observations?

* Autocorrelation does not bias estimated regression coefficients

  + However, multilevel models can also help understand effects single level models cannot when there is autocorrelation
  
* Standard errors of regression coefficients can be underestimated, leading to inflated Type I error rates for $t$ tests of regression coefficients

* Can inflate Type I error rate of $F$ test for $R^2$


## Model Specification

* Scatterplots of residuals ($y$-axis) against predicted outcome values ($x$-axis) with loess line imposed

* Scatterplots of residuals ($y$-axis) against each predictor ($x$-axis) separately, with loess lines imposed
  
* If forms of relationships are properly specified, then loess lines should not exhibit large or systematic deviations from the $y=0$ horizontal line

## Example

```{r}

library(patchwork)

# 1. Simulate data with diminishing returns (logarithmic relationship)
set.seed(101)
n <- 300
x <- runif(n, 1, 10)
y <- 4 * log(x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.75)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# 2. Fit models
# Correctly specified: Account for diminishing returns using log(x)
mod_correct <- lm(y ~ log(x), data = df)
df$res_correct <- residuals(mod_correct)

# Misspecified: Naively fit a simple linear term (lm(y ~ x))
mod_misspec <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
df$res_misspec <- residuals(mod_misspec)

# Shared theme setup
theme_residual <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "grey30"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# 3. Left Panel: Correct Model Residuals vs. Predictor
p_correct <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = res_correct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#2c7bb6") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#2c7bb6", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Correct Specification: log(x)",
    x = "Predictor: log(x)",
    y = "Residuals (y - ŷ)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3.5, 3.5)) +
  theme_residual()

# 4. Right Panel: Misspecified Model Residuals vs. Predictor
p_misspec <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = res_misspec)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "#d7191c") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#d7191c", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Misspecified Model: Linear x",
    x = "Predictor: x",
    y = "Residuals (y - ŷ)"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3.5, 3.5)) +
  theme_residual()

# 5. Assemble side-by-side plot
p_correct + p_misspec
```

## Interpretation

The correct relationship between $x$ and $y$ was not linear for $x$, but was linear for $\text{log}(x)$. If we failed to account for this transformation:


- For small and large values of $x$, residuals tend to be negative
  - We are **overpredicting** $y$
- For medium values of $x$ we are **underpredicting** $y$
- Same pattern (but negative so curve is inverted) can be seen if we don't correctly specify the log of percent SAT in SAT model

```{r}
p3 <- ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x = mod2$model$PctSAT, y = mod2$residuals), color = my_purple) + 
  theme_light() + labs(x = "Percent SAT", y = "Residuals") + 
  geom_smooth(aes(x = mod2$model$PctSAT, y = mod2$residuals), method = "loess", col = my_blue)

grid.arrange(p2, p3, nrow = 1)
```

## Model Spec. Errors

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

| Error | Corr with Outcome | Corr with at least one predictor | Effect on reg coefficients? | Effect on standard errors? |
|:-------------------------|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|:----------------------------|
| Relevant variable omitted (1) | Yes | No | No | Biased standard errors (too large) |
| Relevant variable omitted (2) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Biased standard errors (too small) |
| Irrelevant variable included | No | No | No | Increases standard errors |

Wrong form of relationships fitted:

1. If the relationship is linear, but you add a quadratic term ($x_1^2$), you have added an irrelevant variable

2. If the relationship is quadratic and you omit the quadratic term:

    + If $x_1$ is symmetric, $x_1$ is not correlated with $x_1^2$ $\rightarrow$ "relevant variable omitted (1)"

    + If $x_1$ is very skewed, $x_1$ is correlated with $x_1^2$ $\rightarrow$ "relevant variable omitted (2)"

:::

## Additivity

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

* Regression coefficient: relationship of one predictor to the outcome, when all other predictors are held constant (i.e., partialing out other predictors)
  
* We do not indicate at what specific value each variable is held constant
  
* Rather, the partial relationships should be constant regardless of the values of the other variables that are being held constant
  
* This is called **additivity**, that the relationship of one predictor to the outcome does not depend on specific values of the other variables
  
* Example of non-additivity: moderation (interaction, coming soon!):
  
$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3 (x_1 \times x_2)$$

* Regression slope of $y$ on $x_1$ depends on the value of $x_2$

* Define a new variable ($x_1 \times x_2$) and enter into the regression model that is linear in coefficients

:::

## CTT



Regression (and the other methods we've learned so far) assume that the variables are **perfectly reliable**

The concept of reliability is based on classical test theory (CTT):

$$X = T + e$$

* $X$: Observed score
* $T$: True score (perfectly reliable)
* $e$: Random measurement error

## Reliability

Quantifies proportion of observed score attributable to true score

- Put another way: how free from measurement error is observed score?

$$\text{Reliability } = \sigma^2_T / \sigma^2_X$$



* $\sigma^2_X$: variance of observed $X$ scores
* $\sigma^2_T$: variance of true scores

Reliability ranges from 0 to 1 (perfectly reliable)



## Perfectly Reliability

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Unreliable predictors bias regression coefficients
  
The direction of bias is not always predictable in advance

Single predictor:

* If the predictor is unreliable, its regression coefficient will be closer to zero than in the population

* Underestimated effect size and low statistical power

* Correlations involving an unreliable variable are lower than if the variable is perfectly reliable

Multiple predictors

* Typical, but not necessary, that regression coefficients will be closer to zero

Methods such as **structural equation modeling** often better accommodate variables that are not perfectly reliable

:::

## Multivariate Outliers

We have an intuition as to what constitutes univariate outliers

* A 4'10" adult human

* A 400lb adult human

It is also possible to have **multivariate outliers** - values that are not necessarily unusual for individual variables, but whose combination is unusual

* An adult human who is 6'2" and 120 lbs

## Regression Diagnostics

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Multiple regression is **not** robust to:

* Stray data points that fall far from the swarm of points in the predictor space
* Outcome $y$ values that are unusual, given values of the predictors

These errant points are called **outliers**

* They may have no effect on the regression analysis results
* They may drastically affect the regression analysis results

Three characteristics of data points:

1. **Leverage**: extent to which observation is close to or far from the rest of other observations, [in terms of scores on the predictors only]{.underline}
2. **Distance**: extent to which the observation's score on the [outcome]{.underline} is extreme, [given the values on the set of predictors]{.underline}
3. **Influence**: extent to which a single data point changes the outcome of the regression analysis

:::

## Leverage

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

* Leverage does not consider any information about the outcome

* Leverage reflects the distance of an observation from the centroid of the predictor space

* Leverage reflects the **potential** of the observation to affect the regression results

Leverage statistic $h$ (or "hat"):

* Measure of how far each observation is from the centroid of the predictors

* Think: a $p$-dimensional scatterplot - how far is each observation from the center of mass?

* Leverage values range from $1/N$  to 1

* Take a closer look at leverage values > $3(p+1) / N$

:::

## Leverage

```{r}
dat <- dat |> mutate(logPctSAT = log(PctSAT)) |> column_to_rownames("Abbreviation")  
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

lm2 <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, dat)
round(hatvalues(lm2), 2)
3 * (2 + 1) / 50 # leverage cutoff when p = 2, N = 50
```

Notice any states with high $h$ values?

## Leverage

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false


lm2 <- lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, dat)
round(hatvalues(lm2), 2)
3 * (2 + 1) / 50 # leverage cutoff when p = 2, N = 50
```

```{r}
#| results: asis

options(width = 60)
out <- capture.output({
  print(round(hatvalues(lm2), 2))
  print(3 * (2 + 1) / 50)
})
emit_html(out_block(hl_named_vector(out, "NJ", my_orange)))
```

Notice any states with high $h$ values?

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

One potential outlier in New Jersey - likely flagged for high expenditures

```{r}
#| echo: true

dat |> summarize(Expend_mean = round(mean(Expend),2),
                 logPctSAT_mean = round(mean(logPctSAT),2), 
                 r = round(cor(Expend, logPctSAT),2))

dat |> filter(State == "New Jersey") |> select(Expend, logPctSAT)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(car)

leveragePlots(lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, subdat))

hatvalues(lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, subdat))
cutoff <- 3 / 50
which(hatvalues(lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, subdat)) > cutoff)


influence_results <- influence(lm(SAT ~ Expend + logPctSAT, subdat))
names(influence_results)
# hat: diagonal of the "hat" matrix
# coefficients: change in estimated coefficients when ith case is dropped
# sigma: standard deviation when ith case is omitted
# wt.res: weighted residuals
```

## Distance



High distance reflects unusual $y$ scores, given predictor scores

Measures of distance are based on the **residuals**

Distance measures (for each observation):

* Raw/unstandardized residuals ($y - \hat{y}$)

    + Not very informative because no suggested cutoff recommended
    + No general cutoff because residuals are in the units of $y$
    + Not suggested
    
## Standardized Distance

Two Types:

* Internally studentized residuals

$$\frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{MS_{\text{residual}}\times (1 - h)}}$$

* Externally studentized residuals
  
$$\frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{MS_{\text{residual}(i)}\times (1 - h)}}$$



## Internal Studentization




::::: columns

:::: {.column width="70%"}

$$\frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{MS_{\text{residual}}\times (1 - h)}}$$

::::

:::: {.column width="30%"}

::: {style="border: 3px solid #4DAF4A; color: #4DAF4A; padding: 0.3em 0.6em;"}
$h$: leverage values
:::
::: {style="border: 3px solid #377EB8; color: #377EB8; padding: 0.3em 0.6em;"}
$MS_{\text{residual}}$ is the squared residual standard error
:::


::::

:::::

* Numerator ($y - \hat{y}$) and denominator ($MS_\text{residual}$) are not independent
* If observation greatly affects regression, $MS_\text{residual}$ will be affected
* Not recommended



## External Studentization



::::: columns

:::: {.column width="70%"}

$$\frac{y - \hat{y}}{\sqrt{MS_{\text{residual}(i)}\times (1 - h)}}$$

::::

:::: {.column width="30%"}

::: {style="border: 3px solid #4DAF4A; color: #4DAF4A; padding: 0.3em 0.6em;"}
$h$: leverage values
:::
::: {style="border: 3px solid #377EB8; color: #377EB8; padding: 0.3em 0.6em;"}
$MS_{\text{residual}}$ is the squared residual standard error
:::
::::

:::::
  
* $MS_{\text{residual}(i)} = MS_{\text{residual}}$ using dataset without target observation $i$
* Independent numerator and denominator
* Suggested cutoff: if > 2.5 in absolute value, outstanding distance
* Recommended distance measure


## Distance

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Raw residuals (output omitted):

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

residuals(lm2)
```

Internally studentized residuals (output omitted):

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

rstandard(lm2)
```

Externally studentized residuals:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

(distance_measure <- rstudent(lm2))
```

```{r}
#| results: asis

# Output of the code above, with the state flagged for distance (WV) circled in orange
distance_measure <- rstudent(lm2)
op <- options(width = 70, digits = 2)
out <- capture.output(print(distance_measure))
options(op)
emit_html(out_block(hl_named_vector(out, "WV", my_orange)))
```

:::

## Influence

An observation might have high leverage or high distance and still not affect the position of the regression plane

Influence is the extent to which an observation actually changes the regression results

Influence is a function of both leverage and distance

Influence measures:

* DFFITS

* DFBETA

* Cook's distance

* COVRATIO

## DFFITS

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Influence measures (for each observation):
  
DFFITS: global measure of standardized change in predicted scores

$$\text{DFFITS} = \frac{\hat{y} - \hat{y}_{(i)}}{s_{\hat{y}_{(i)}}}$$

* $\hat{y}$: predicted outcome for observation $i$ when observation $i$ is included in the regression
* $\hat{y}_{(i)}$: predicted outcome for observation $i$ when observation $i$ is excluded from the regression (use fitted model to predict the outcome)
* $s_{\hat{y}_{(i)}}$ standard error of $\hat{y}_{(i)}$
* DFFITS reflects how much the regression line changes if observation $i$ is deleted
* Suggested cutoffs:
    + Moderate $N$: absolute DFFITS > 1, outstanding influence
    + Large $N$: absolute DFFITS > $2\sqrt{(p+1)/N}$, outstanding influence

:::

## DFFITS Viz

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

ggplot(tibble(index = 1:50, DFFITS = dffits(mod), Abbr = rownames(dat)), aes(index, DFFITS)) + 
  geom_blank() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = Abbr), hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 4) + 
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = .4898979), col = my_blue) + 
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = -.4898979), col = my_blue) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 0.57, hjust = 0, size = 6, color = my_green, parse = TRUE,
           label = "bold(2*sqrt((p+1)/N) ~ '=' ~ 2*sqrt(3/50) ~ '=' ~ '.49')")
```

## DFBETAS

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Influence measures (for each observation):
  
DFBETAS: measures the standardized change in regression coefficients

$$\text{DFBETAS} = \frac{b - b_{(i)}}{s_{b_{(i)}}}$$

* $b$: regression coefficient when observation $i$ is included in the regression

* $b_{(i)}$: regression coefficient when observation $i$ is excluded from the regression

* $s_{b_{(i)}}$ standard error of $b_{(i)}$

Suggested cutoffs:
  
* Moderate sample size: absolute DFBETAS > 1, outstanding influence

* Large sample size: absolute DFBETAS > $2/\sqrt{N}$, outstanding influence

:::

## DFBETAS viz

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5

DFBETAS <- as.data.frame(dfbetas(mod))
DFBETAS <- DFBETAS |> 
  pivot_longer("(Intercept)":"logPctSAT", names_to = "Coefficient", values_to = "DFBETAS") |>
  mutate(index = rep(1:50, 3), Abbr = rep(rownames(dat), 3))
ggplot(DFBETAS, aes(index, DFBETAS)) + 
  geom_blank() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = Abbr), hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.5) + 
  facet_wrap(~Coefficient) + 
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = 0.2828427), col = my_blue) + 
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = -0.2828427), col = my_blue)
```

## Others

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Influence measures (for each observation):

* Cook's Distance: Global measure of influence
  
    + Closely related to DFFITS, but with squared differences

    + Suggested cutoff: $D > 1$ indicates influential point

* COVRATIO

    + Global measure of influence based on sizes of standard error of each regression coefficient when observation $i$ is included/excluded from regression analysis

    + Smaller covratio, more stable regression coefficients (smaller standard errors)

    + Suggested cutoff: |covratio - 1|$\geq 3p/N$  indicates less stable regression coefficients

:::

## Influence

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5.5

p1 <- ggplot(tibble(index = 1:50, Cook = cooks.distance(mod), Abbr = rownames(dat)), aes(index, Cook)) + 
  geom_blank() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = Abbr), hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.5)

p2 <- ggplot(tibble(index = 1:50, COVRATIO = covratio(mod), Abbr = rownames(dat)), aes(index, COVRATIO)) + 
  geom_blank() + theme_minimal() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = Abbr), hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.5) + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.12, col = my_blue)

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1)
```

## Summary



Diagnostics usually consider one observation at a time

Some suggested strategies:

* Look at global influence DFFITS first. Look for observations with DFFITS > $2 \sqrt{(p+1)/N}$

* For these observations, look at all the DFBETAS. Be concerned if DFBETAS > 1
  
* Examine these observations for data entry errors (or other errors unrelated to the study)
  
* Unless a strong case can be made for deleting the observation, the observation stays
